events.credibility_reason: The two-prime claim would imply Brocard only through a counting step that the source does not make. The 2025 commentary says the proofs rest partly on facts most number theorists would call conjectures, and a 2026 review states that no unconditional two-prime result is known.
Withdrawn (v7). The arXiv admin note cites pseudonymous authorship.
One short preprint claims eleven famous conjectures. It rests on the author's own claimed proof of Firoozbakht's conjecture and on the open Oppermann conjecture. No engagement in about 10 years.
A single-version claimed proof of Legendre's conjecture. The only objection is from an automated referee, seen second-hand.
A self-posted ScienceOpen claim of a landmark result with no engagement in about 5 years. Later sources (MathWorld 2025, Wikipedia) still call the conjecture unproven, and the text was unreadable.
The page states both that it proves Andrica's conjecture and that no verified solution exists. Later versions are reported as conditional.

Claims Oppermann, Andrica, Legendre and Brocard at once, which would be a landmark, with no engagement in 26 months. The method changed across four versions in a month, and at least one version is conditional on an unproven inequality. The same author's Andrica note follows the same pattern, and a 2026 review still treats these conjectures as open.

The unconditional Theorem 6.8 would settle a strong form of Legendre's conjecture, yet the same paper calls Legendre open and derives the weaker one-prime statement only conditionally. The prerequisite Theorem 6.6 has no proof that could be found, and Section 6.1 invokes Legendre's conjecture. There has been no uptake in 22 months on a landmark claim, and the 2026 Chamberland-Straub review states that no unconditional two-prime result exists. The paper never draws the Brocard conclusion; it comes from the researcher's inference.
Self-reported with no proof text, and it concerns the namesake equation.
A forum participant identified a specific error in a claimed step (counterexample at n = 32, A = 17), and it has not been answered.

why: The only events after the snapshot that claim the whole statement are Vega's Oppermann note and Grah's preprint. Both are set aside as not credible, because several F10 signals are present at once, not merely because nobody has reviewed them. Grah was the closest call. The step from Proposition 6.11 to Brocard (d_n >= 2, so at least four primes) is sound if Theorem 6.8 holds. But Theorem 6.8 contradicts the paper's own treatment of Legendre's conjecture as open, its prerequisite Theorem 6.6 is unproved in the text available, nobody has engaged with it in 22 months on a landmark, and a 2026 review states that no such result is known. Taken together, these signals outweigh treating it as merely doubtful. The MathWorld/OEIS check and Visser's check are finite instances. The Brocard-Ramanujan items, the Legendre, Andrica and almost-prime results, and Tyszka are variants. Clements names Claude Sonnet 3.7, but systems[] is empty and the model only suggested a namesake problem, so ai_role is none. Before the snapshot, every claim of the whole statement is unreviewed, withdrawn or not credible, so none of them tiers as resolved.
doubts: Grah's Theorem 6.6 and its acknowledgements were not read (the HTML copy was truncated), so both the credibility call and the AI check on Grah rest on partial text. Grah's paper does not itself draw the >= 4 conclusion. For Spencer-Brown, the scope of 'whole' depends on the same counting inference. Naciri's date is year-only (2025), but it lies after the snapshot regardless; it was set to null only to follow the year-only rule, and it is a variant either way.
